1918.title: who-iris
1918.content: Measured from who-iris/translations, that instance's own translation-sources directory. Scroll horizontally to see all columns → . | locale | catalogues / templatesQ1: availability | entriesQ2: strings | translated | fuzzy | untranslated | officialQ3: signed off | . | ar Arabic | 2 / 633.3% · view files → | 160 | 160100% | 0 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . | es Spanish | 2 / 633.3% · view files → | 160 | 160100% | 0 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . | fr French | 2 / 633.3% · view files → | 160 | 160100% | 0 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . | ru Russian | 2 / 633.3% · view files → | 160 | 160100% | 0 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . | zh Chinese | 2 / 633.3% · view files → | 160 | 160100% | 0 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . Two questions, not one. catalogues / templates asks whether a .po exists at all for each extractable .pot; the string columns ask how much of the catalogues that DO exist is done. A locale can be near 100% translated across a handful of catalogues while most of its templates have none — which is why the first column is not folded into the rest. “no basis” is not zero. A share over an empty denominator is undefined, and rendering it as 0% would report a measurement this run did not make. One directory per table, each named. translation-sources is a graph KIND, and more than one instance may declare it; the first table measures the directory named in the subtitle, and each instance below it gets its own table for its own declared directory. They are never summed: two instances' catalogues answer two questions. A catalogue sitting in an instance that has not declared the directory is invisible here — which is a gap in that declaration rather than a locale with no work done, and the two must not read the same. Fuzzy is counted apart from translated. A fuzzy entry has a translation and needs review; adding it to translated would flatter exactly the entries a reviewer must look at.

1968.title: Business Process candidate
1968.content: A set of activities and tasks performed in coordination to achieve a specified business objective, or to deliver value in a specific way to a health service user. In the context of digitizing care pathways, this could include “health service user registration” and “referrals”, for example (see section 3.3). Also called: business process . PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 8). Wording alternative in SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9, citing DIIG): "A set of related activities or tasks performed together to achieve the objectives of the health programme area, such as registration, counselling and referrals (3)." Both are recorded as candidates; neither is chosen.

1973.title: Functional Application candidate
1973.content: Functional applications are application components that deliver a specific operational function within a defined domain. They are context-specific, reflecting the operational requirements of a programme, scheme, or institution that procures them. Also called: Functional application . The RA draft's own wording, verbatim. A candidate until the RA editors adopt it through the public review.

1978.title: Semantic Governance Infrastructure (SGI) candidate
1978.content: The Semantic Governance Infrastructure (SGI) is the cross-cutting capability that keeps the metadata registry components accurate, consistent and trustworthy, so that the semantic consistency they are intended to provide does not degrade as the health digital ecosystem grows. 2018.title: Digital Transformation candidate
2018.content: The process of digitally optimizing and driving systems-level changes by leveraging innovation, analytics and feedback mechanisms to improve person-centred health systems. Digital technologies are used to fundamentally change and improve how health services are delivered and accessed across all health programme areas (12,14,15). Also called: digital transformation . PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 8); identical wording (with minor punctuation/citation differences) in PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9). Wording alternative in SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8), which inverts the two sentences: "In the health context, using digital technologies to fundamentally change and improve how health services are delivered and accessed across all health programme areas (3, 4, 5). The process involves using innovation, analytics and feedback mechanisms to achieve systems-level changes." All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1).

2029.title: Data Dictionary candidate
2029.content: A singular storage location for information about the data elements, detailing their type and definition, relationships, origin and use. Also called: data dictionary . PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 8). Wording alternative in SFP handbook §4.4 body (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-025-44-outline-data-requirements.md, page-042.md, p. 30): "A data dictionary is a repository of information about the data elements such as description, data type and other characteristics." Both are recorded as candidates; neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, dth-sfp#1 P2).

2045.title: Client Registry (CR) candidate
2045.content: The Client Registry is the national authoritative source of health-specific person identity. It is the foundational health-sector component that maintains a unique, verifiable identity record for every person who accesses or is eligible to access health services within a jurisdiction. Also called: CR . Verbatim lead sentence from Appendix C (Client Registry, 1 What It Is). Also abbreviated CR in the OpenHIE requirement identifiers (CRF-*, CRWF-*) and downstream Digital Transformation Handbooks. A candidate until the RA editors adopt it through the public review.

2050.title: Enterprise Architecture (EA) candidate
2050.content: The organising logic for business processes and IT infrastructure reflecting the integration and standardisation requirements of the organisation's operating model. Also called: EA, enterprise architecture . The RA draft's own glossary wording, verbatim (folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md); the draft marks this entry [Under review]. Substantive alternatives across the DTH corpus (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#140): (1) PHC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 9, citing DIIG): "A blueprint of business processes, data, systems and technologies used to help planners, software developers and managers design increasingly complex systems to support the workflow and roles of people in a large enterprise, such as a health system (11)." (2) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8, citing DIIG): "A blueprint of business processes, data, systems and technologies that helps planners, software developers and managers design increasingly complex systems to support the workflow and roles of people in a large enterprise such as a health system (1)." (3) SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9, citing DIIG): "A blueprint of business processes, data, systems and technologies used to help implementers design increasingly complex systems to support the workflow and roles of people in a large enterprise, such as a health system (3)." All four are recorded as candidates; none is chosen.

2075.title: Registry candidate
2075.content: A governed, authoritative and centralized information system that captures, stores and maintains the unique attributes and identifiers of health facilities, health service users, health products and/or the health workforce using a predefined canonical minimum data set. Also called: registry . The RA draft's own glossary wording, verbatim (folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md); the draft marks this entry [Under review]. Near-identical wording alternatives across the DTH corpus (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#142): (1) PHC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 11): "A governed, authoritative and centralized information system that captures, stores and maintains the unique attributes and identifiers of health-care facilities, health service users, products and/or health workforce using a predefined canonical minimum data set." (2) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "A governed, authoritative and centralized information system that captures, stores and maintains the unique attributes and identifiers of health facilities, health service users, health products and/or the health workforce using a predefined canonical minimum data set." (3) PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "A governed, authoritative and centralized information system that captures, stores, and maintains the unique attributes and identifiers of health facilities, health service users, products and/or health workforce using a predefined canonical minimum data set." (4) SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-010.md, p. 10, truncated in source PDF): "A governed, authoritative and centralized information system that captures, stores and maintains the unique attributes and identifiers of health facilities, health service users, products and/or health workforce using predefined canonical minimum data etc." All five are recorded as candidates; none is chosen.

2085.title: Product Master Data (PMD) candidate
2085.content: Product master data consists of standardized information that accurately describes a health product’s characteristics. This data remains consistent across all instances of a product. Also called: PMD, product master data . PC handbook Introduction wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-010.md, p. 10). Shared concept across PC (9789240116191-eng), SC (9789240101197-eng), and SFP (9789240120747-eng). Per owner decision 2026-10-31 (smart-ra#141, smart-ra#142): one concept, with no homonym split needed against the RA's architectural `product` concept.

2091.title: Product candidate
2091.content: A concrete offering, bundling services and data, that is made available to stakeholders. The RA draft's own glossary wording, verbatim (folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md). Wording alternative in RA Table 3.1 (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-026-31-the-architecture-description-approach.md): "A coherent offering that bundles services and data for use by stakeholders." Note: in the PC (9789240116191-eng) and SFP (9789240120747-eng) handbooks, the bare word 'product' is used as a synonym for `generic-product` (a health product / medicine); per owner decision 2026-10-31 (smart-ra#142), `product-master-data` and `generic-product` are separate concepts and no homonym split is needed on Product Master Data.

2106.title: Benefits Package Registry (BPR) candidate
2106.content: The Benefits Package Registry is the national authoritative record of all health benefit packages offered within a country's health financing ecosystem. It holds the definitive description of what each package covers, who is eligible in general terms, which scheme or schemes offer it, and under what rules and conditions benefits may be accessed. Also called: BPR . Verbatim lead sentences from Appendix C (Benefits Package Registry, 1 What It Is). Abbreviated BPR in the Appendix C comparison table. A candidate until the RA editors adopt it through the public review.

2136.title: Logical Information Model Repository (LIMR) candidate
2136.content: The Logical Information Model Repository is a governed, publicly accessible repository and management platform for computable clinical and administrative information models that define the logical structure, semantics, and terminology bindings of health data objects across a national digital health ecosystem. Also called: LIMR . Verbatim lead sentence from Appendix C (Logical Information Model Repository, 1 What It Is). Abbreviated LIMR throughout the RA draft. A candidate until the RA editors adopt it through the public review.

2201.title: Functional Requirements candidate
2201.content: Description of what the digital system needs to do to support the tasks that make up the health system process and address the identified health system challenges (e.g. a PCPOSS must be able to remind health workers which health service users to follow-up with). Also called: functional requirements, Functional requirements . PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 9). Wording and substantive alternatives across the DTH corpus (smart-ra#133 S1): (1) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "A description of what the digital system needs to do to support the tasks that make up the business process and address the identified challenges." (2) PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "Description of what the digital system needs to do to support the tasks that make up the health system process and address the identified challenges (e.g., a product master data management solution must be able to define categories and attributes to organize product information)." (3) SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "Capabilities the system must have to meet the end users’ needs and achieve tasks within the business process." All four are recorded as candidates; none is chosen.

2223.title: Workflow candidate
2223.content: The sequence of activities from one task to another (see section 3.3). Also called: workflow . PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 11). Internal and cross-DTH alternatives (smart-ra#133 S1): (1) PHC handbook §3.3 body (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-014-33-map-business-processes-and-workflows.md, pp. 35-39): "Workflows are a visual representation of the progression of activities (tasks, events, interactions) performed within a business process (45)." (2) SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-011.md, p. 11, citing DIIG/DAK): "A visual representation of the progression of activities (tasks, events, decision points) in a logical flow illustrating the interactions within the business process (21)." (PHC glossary defines a workflow as the sequence of activities itself; PHC §3.3 and SFP glossary define it as the visual representation of that progression.) All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen.

2238.title: Traceability candidate
2238.content: The ability to trace something. In some cases, it is interpreted as the ability to verify the history, location or application of an item by means of documented identification (14). Also called: traceability . SC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9, citing the WHO policy paper on traceability of medical products, ref. 14). Internal/substantive alternative in SC handbook Ch. 4 boxed definition (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-054.md, p. 54, citing GS1): "Traceability is the ability to trace the history, application or location of an object. In a supply chain context, it is the ability to see the movement of health products across the supply chain." Shared across dth-sc, dth-pc, and dth-sfp; both definitions are recorded as candidates and neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#140).

2258.title: Non-Functional Requirements (NFR) candidate
2258.content: General attributes and features of the digital system to ensure usability and overcome technical and physical constraints. Examples of non-functional requirements include ability to work offline, multiple language settings, and password protection (see section 3.8). Also called: Non-functional requirements, nonfunctional requirements, NFR . PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 10), identical (without section cross-reference) in SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-010.md, p. 10). Substantive alternatives across the DTH corpus (smart-ra#133 S1): (1) SC handbook glossary ('nonfunctional requirements', who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "A description of how the digital system needs to operate and perform in order to support the tasks that make up the business process." (2) PC handbook glossary ('Non-functional requirements', who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "Description of the attributes and constraints that the system must have to ensure its quality and performance. These requirements do not specify what the system should do, but rather how the system should perform its functions. (e.g., a product master data management solution must be able to support offline mode when network connectivity is not available)" All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen.

2295.title: Governance candidate
2295.content: Governance is the set of arrangements through which decision authority is distributed, exercised and accounted for across all those who depend upon, contribute to, or are served by the shared infrastructure. Also called: governance, governance (health supply chain) . RA §3.4.1 body wording, verbatim (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-029-341-purpose-and-framing.md, p. 64–65). Substantive alternative in SC handbook Ch. 3 boxed definition (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-045.md, p. 45): "In the context of the health supply chain, governance is the process of establishing and implementing policies, procedures and mechanisms to ensure that the supply chain processes and the systems to manage those processes are managed effectively, ethically and in alignment with established objectives and stakeholders’ interests." (RA defines governance as the distribution, exercise, and accountability of decision authority across shared infrastructure; SC defines it as the process of establishing and implementing policies, procedures, and mechanisms for supply chain processes and systems.) Also related to `digital-health-governance` in Mehl et al. 2023 (glossary/full-stac.glossary.json, smart-ra#143 P8). Also framed in SFP handbook §2.3 (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-015-23-establish-governance-and-leadership.md, page-028.md, p. 16) as a structure for coordinating multiple stakeholders, defining clear roles and responsibilities, enhancing transparency, and creating a stable platform for decision-making. Both definitions are recorded as candidates; neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#140, dth-sfp#1 P2).

2317.title: Health Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI-H) candidate
2317.content: Health Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI-H) refers to digital resources that are built as a shared means for fulfilling multiple health agency functions. Also called: DPI-H, HDPI . The RA draft's own glossary wording, verbatim (folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md). Wording alternative in RA §1.1.2 body (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-002-112-understanding-digital-public-infrastructure.md), which adds a second defining sentence: "Health Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI-H) refers to digital resources that are built as a shared means for fulfilling multiple health agency functions. These digital resources for health — encompassing both systems and specifications — leverage foundational DPI, are interoperable, reusable, publicly governed and built on open standards." Both are recorded as candidates; neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1).

2332.title: Monitoring candidate
2332.content: The continuous process of collecting and analysing data to compare how well an intervention is being implemented against expected results (8). Also called: monitoring . SFP handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-010.md, p. 10, citing Monitoring and evaluating digital health interventions, WHO 2016). Wording alternative in DIIG Annex 1.1 Glossary (who-iris/library/9789240010567-eng/sections/page-141.md, p. 129, citing WHO evaluation practice handbook, 2013): "The process of collecting and analysing routinely collected data to compare how well an intervention is being implemented against expected results and measure changes in performance over time." Both definitions are recorded as candidates; neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, dth-sfp#1 §2.1 Cluster B1).

2374.title: Stakeholder candidate
2374.content: An individual, role, or organisation with an interest in the outcomes of the architecture. Also called: stakeholder . The RA draft's own glossary wording, verbatim (folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md). Substantive and wording alternatives across the corpus (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#140): (1) RA Table 3.1 (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-026-31-the-architecture-description-approach.md): "An individual, team, or organisation with interests in, or concerns relative to, the architecture." (2) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "In the context of digital health transformation, anyone who is affected by or interested in the consequences of the efforts, including the planning team, end users, beneficiaries and funders." (4) DIIG Annex 1.1 Glossary (who-iris/library/9789240010567-eng/sections/page-141.md, p. 129): "Any person who is affected by or interested in the consequences of the digital health implementation; stakeholders include the planning team, end-users, beneficiaries and funders." (Also enumerated in SFP handbook §1.1, who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-009-11-analyse-key-stakeholders.md, page-020.md, p. 8.) All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen.

2379.content: Open architectures refer to high-level specifications of technical designs that provide blueprints for creating open ecosystems structured into reusable and shareable components. Linked via exactMatch to the full-STAC scheme (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#143).

2401.title: Systems Architecture candidate
2401.content: The technical framework of the system depicted in a conceptual model that defines how the system is structured and how its elements are connected. Also called: systems architecture, system architecture . PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 11). Wording alternative in SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "A technical framework based on a conceptual model that defines how the system should be structured and how its elements should be connected." Internal alternative in PHC handbook §4.4 body under 'system architecture' (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-023-44-design-system-architecture.md, pp. 56-60): "A system architecture is a conceptual model that depicts how the PCPOSS will be structured and how it functions and includes all the software and hardware components that comprise the system." All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#200).

2412.title: Interoperability candidate
2412.content: Interoperability is the standards-based capability of heterogeneous information systems to communicate, exchange data, and use the exchanged information to execute functions effectively. Also called: interoperability . The RA draft's own glossary wording, verbatim (folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md). Substantive and internal alternatives across the DTH corpus (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#140, smart-ra#142): (1) PHC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 9), PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8), and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-010.md, p. 10): "Ability of different applications to access, exchange, integrate and use data in a coordinated and consistent manner through the use of shared application interfaces, value sets, concepts and standards, within and across organizational, regional and national boundaries, to provide timely and seamless portability of information and optimize health outcomes." (2) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8, citing DIIG): "The ability of different applications to access, exchange, integrate and use data in a coordinated and consistent manner, through the use of shared application interfaces, value sets, concepts and standards within and across organizational, regional and national boundaries. In the health context, this provides timely, safe and seamless portability of information to help ensure good health outcomes (1)." (3) PHC handbook §4.4 body (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-023-44-design-system-architecture.md, §4.4, pp. 56-60): "Interoperability is the ability of different applications to access, exchange, integrate and use data in a coordinated manner through the use of shared application interfaces and standards, which should be defined by the EA and independent of a particular solution’s system architecture (22)." (4) PHC handbook §4.4.2 body (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-023-44-design-system-architecture.md, pp. 56-60): "Interoperability is the ability of different applications to access, exchange, integrate and use data in a coordinated manner through the use of shared application interfaces and data representation standards, within and across organizational, regional and national boundaries, to provide timely and seamless portability of information and optimize health outcomes." All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen.

2417.title: Evaluation candidate
2417.content: The systematic and objective assessment of an ongoing or completed intervention with the aim of determining the fulfilment of objectives, efficiency, effectiveness, impact and sustainability (8). Also called: evaluation . SFP handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-009.md, p. 9, citing Monitoring and evaluating digital health interventions, WHO 2016). Wording alternative in DIIG Annex 1.1 Glossary (who-iris/library/9789240010567-eng/sections/page-140.md, p. 128, citing WHO evaluation practice handbook, 2013): "The systematic assessment of an ongoing or completed intervention to determine whether the intervention is fulfilling its objectives and to demonstrate an effect on health outcomes." Also contrasted with monitoring in SFP §6.1 (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-029-61-develop-a-monitoring-and-evaluation-plan.md, page-051.md, p. 39, quoting Pritchett et al. 2013): "Evaluation asks whether the project is doing the right things, while monitoring asks whether the project is doing things right." Both definitions are recorded as candidates; neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, dth-sfp#1 §2.1 Cluster B1).

2443.title: Capability candidate
2443.content: A high-level ability the health system possesses or needs in order to achieve its goals. It expresses what the health system is able to do, independently of how that ability is implemented. The RA draft's own glossary wording, verbatim (folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md). Wording alternative in RA Table 3.1 (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-026-31-the-architecture-description-approach.md): "An ability that an organisation, person, or system possesses — expressed in terms of what can be done, not how or by whom." Both are recorded as candidates; neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1).

2448.title: Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) candidate
2448.content: A set of shared digital systems that should be secure and interoperable, and can be built on open standards and specifications to deliver and provide equitable access to public and/or private services at societal scale and are governed by applicable legal frameworks and enabling rules to drive development, inclusion, innovation, trust, and competition, while respecting human rights and fundamental freedoms. (G20/UNDP) . Also called: DPI . The RA draft's own glossary wording, verbatim (folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md). Wording alternative in RA §1.1.2 body (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-002-112-understanding-digital-public-infrastructure.md): "Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) refers to shared digital systems that are secure and interoperable, built on open standards and specifications to deliver and provide equitable access to public and/or private services at societal scale and are governed by applicable legal frameworks and enabling rules to drive development, inclusion, innovation, trust, and competition and respect human rights and fundamental freedoms." (Glossary reads "interoperable, and can be built"; body reads "interoperable, built".) Both are recorded as candidates; neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1).

2453.title: Trade Item candidate
2453.content: Trade items are manufacturer-specific branded health products that are identifiable and unique to a particular brand or manufacturer. Also called: trade item, Trade item . Owner decision 2026-10-31 (smart-ra#142 item 1, smart-ra#139): Trade Item is the shared WHO concept with this narrow definition from the Product Catalogue handbook Ch. 2 body (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-028.md, p. 28). The GS1 trade item is a separate external concept and the WHO term's broadMatch (every WHO Trade Item is a GS1 trade item, not the reverse: GS1's also covers services). The PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-011.md, p. 11) print the GS1 wording — "Products or services that are priced, ordered or invoiced at any point in the supply chain" — citing GS1 (PC ref. 13, SFP ref. 19); that sentence is recorded here as a note citing GS1, not as the WHO concept's definition.

2482.title: Functions candidate
2482.content: Functions in a system are how features are implemented (e.g. “calculating aggregate data” and “displaying feedback in the form of diagrams” are functions of the “reporting” feature of a PCPOSS). Also called: functions . PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 9). Substantive alternative in SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "Business processes within a system that help the system perform (e.g., “receiving inventory” and “picking inventory” are functions of the “warehousing” feature of a warehouse management system)." (PHC defines functions as "how features are implemented"; SC defines them as "Business processes within a system that help the system perform".) Both are recorded as candidates; neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1).

2503.title: Foundational Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI-F) candidate
2503.content: Foundational Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI-F) is the digital public infrastructure, such as identity, payments and data exchange, upon which the health sector can build. DPI-H is distinct from DPI-F and builds on it. Also called: DPI-F . Added to the RA glossary table in CS-001 (smart-ra#185, public comments No. 136 and No. 327), per committee feedback (CL). A candidate until the RA editors adopt it through the public review. Named in the RA draft's Acronyms table, which gives the expansion used as prefLabel, and in Section 1.2.3 on cross-sectoral foundational DPI (digital identity, payments, data exchange).

2513.title: SMART Guidelines (SMART) candidate
2513.content: Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based, Testable Guidelines are a comprehensive set of reusable digital health components (e.g., interoperability standards, code libraries, algorithms, technical and operational specifications) that transform the guideline adaptation and implementation process to preserve fidelity and accelerate uptake. SMART Guidelines provide a five-step pathway to advance the adoption of best clinical and data practices, even if a country is not yet fully digital. Also called: SMART guidelines, SMART, Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based, Testable Guidelines . The RA draft's own glossary wording, verbatim (folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md). Substantive and wording alternatives across the DTH corpus (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#140, smart-ra#142): (1) PHC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 11) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-011.md, p. 11): "Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based, and Testable Guidelines are recommended digital capabilities, health and data content aligned with normative recommendations. They represent packages of comprehensive documentation and reusable digital health components (e.g. health content, interoperability standards, code libraries, algorithms, technical and operational specifications) that facilitate country adaptation and adoption of clinical and public health protocols, health systems strengthening recommendations, and data and interoperability standards into digital health information systems with fidelity. SMART Guidelines serve as a starting point and as foundational specifications to advance the development of robust person-centred digital systems. These specifications are software-agnostic, context-agnostic, and are applicable to all levels of digital maturity (10,23)." (2) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "The WHO guidelines for developing Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based and Testable components for implementing digital health capabilities. The components include interoperability standards, code libraries, algorithms, and technical and operational specifications. The SMART Guidelines provide a five-step pathway to advance the adoption of best clinical and data practices, even if a country is not yet fully digital (12, 13)." (3) PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "WHO standards-based, machine-readable, adaptive, requirements-based, and testable Guidelines are recommended digital capabilities, health and data content. They represent a comprehensive set of reusable digital health components (e.g., interoperability standards, code libraries, algorithms, technical and operational specifications) that transform the guideline adaptation and implementation process to preserve fidelity and accelerate uptake. SMART Guidelines provide a five-step pathway to advance the adoption of best clinical and data practices, even if a country is not yet fully digital.11, 12" All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen.

2550.content: The Computable Decision Support Engine is a governed, shared application component that delivers context-appropriate, evidence-based guidance at the point of clinical decision-making by applying computable clinical rules and knowledge artefacts to person-specific health data. Also called: CDSE . Verbatim lead sentence from Appendix C (Computable Decision Support Engine, 1 What It Is). Abbreviated CDSE throughout the RA draft. A candidate until the RA editors adopt it through the public review.

2580.title: Actor (Conformance Model) candidate
2580.content: An Actor is an abstract, well-bounded role in the health information ecosystem that is defined entirely by the information-processing responsibilities it assumes and the interactions it participates in. An Actor is neither a software product nor an organisational unit. Also called: Actor, actor (conformance model) . Defined in RA §3.7.2 (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-050-372-the-model.md, p. 111–116). Substantive distinction from the platform's `actor` concept in folio-assistant-core/glossary/cat-harness.glossary.json ("A concrete participant, human, agentic or mechanical, that persists across every process and takes on roles"): the RA's conformance-model Actor is an abstract information-processing role realised by concrete systems, closer to IHE's Actor or the platform's Role (smart-ra#133 S1).

2595.content: The Lifelong Health Record (LHR) is one or more governed data repositories, whether physically consolidated or virtually federated, that collectively maintain a longitudinal, person-centred record of an individual's key health information across care settings and over their lifetime. Also called: LHR . Verbatim lead sentence from Appendix C (Lifelong Health Record, 1 What It Is). Abbreviated LHR throughout the RA draft. A candidate until the RA editors adopt it through the public review.

2605.content: Open technologies denote components of configurable and extensible source code — often curated as digital public goods — that perform distinct functions while adhering to open standards. 2617.title: Product Registry (PR) candidate
2617.content: The Product Registry is the national authoritative source of core identity and classification data for health products — medicines, vaccines, medical devices, diagnostics, and health commodities — recognised for use within a jurisdiction. 2622.title: Features candidate
2622.content: The characteristics of a system that include look and feel as well as what the system can do (e.g. “reporting” can be a feature of a PCPOSS). Also called: features . PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 9). Wording alternatives across the DTH corpus, differing only in domain example and 'a system' vs 'your system' (smart-ra#133 S1): (1) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "The characteristics of a system that include look and feel as well as what the system can do (e.g., “order processing” can be a feature of an order management solution)." (2) PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "The characteristics of your system that include look and feel as well as what the system can do (e.g., “approval workflow” can be a feature of a product master data management solution)." All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen.

2633.title: Health Workforce Registry (HWR) candidate
2633.content: The Health Workforce Registry is the national authoritative record of identity, credential, and classification data for all health workers recognised as part of the national health workforce — including licensed or certified clinical professionals, community health workers, allied health personnel, and administrative and management staff in health-related roles. Also called: HWR, Health Worker Registry . Verbatim lead sentence from Appendix C (Health Workforce Registry, 1 What It Is). Also called Health Worker Registry (HWR) in OpenHIE alignment notes and downstream Digital Transformation Handbooks. A candidate until the RA editors adopt it through the public review.

2678.title: Digital Health candidate
2678.content: The systematic application of information and communications technologies, computer science, and data to support informed decision-making by individuals, the health workforce, and health systems, to strengthen resilience to disease and improve health and wellness. Also called: digital health . The RA draft's own glossary wording, verbatim (folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md). Substantive and wording alternatives across the DTH corpus (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#140): (1) PHC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 8, citing WHO Global Strategy on Digital Health 2020–2025): "Digital health is the systematic application of information and communications technologies, computer science, and data to support informed decision-making by individuals, the health workforce, and health systems, to strengthen resilience to disease and improve health and wellness (11)." (2) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8, citing DIIG and Global Strategy): "The systematic application of information and communications technologies, computer science and data to support informed decision-making by individuals, the health workforce and health systems, to strengthen resilience to disease and improve health and wellness (1, 2)." (3) SC handbook Introduction (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-012.md, p. 12, quoting the WHO Global Strategy on Digital Health 2020–2025, same source cited by dth-hrh): "the field of knowledge and practice associated with the development and use of digital technologies to improve health". All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen.

2703.title: Open Source candidate
2703.content: Open-source software is software with source code that is published and made freely available to the public, enabling anyone to inspect, modify and enhance the code (18). While the source code is open to everyone, this does not mean that implementation of software is necessarily without costs. An open-source software must have a license approved by the Open Source Initiative (19). Also called: Open-source software, open-source software, open source . PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 10), identical (with minor punctuation/citation differences) in PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-010.md, p. 10). Wording alternative in SC handbook glossary under 'open-source software' (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8), which adds "within set guidelines": "Software with source code that is published and made freely available to the public so anyone can inspect, modify and enhance the code within set guidelines (8). While the source code is open to everyone, the implementation of the software is not necessarily without costs. Open-source software must have a license approved by the Open Source Initiative (9)." All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1).

2733.title: Generic Product candidate
2733.content: In this handbook, the terms ‘generic product,’ ‘product,’ or ‘product information’ pertain to the general identifying details of a health product, excluding any manufacturer-specific information. Also called: Generic product or product information, product information, generic national product code . PC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8), identical in SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-010.md, p. 10). Internal wording alternative in PC handbook Ch. 2 body (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-028.md, p. 28): "Generic products can be described as generic items that conceal the brand or manufacturer information." Distinct from the RA's architectural `product` concept; both wordings are recorded as candidates and neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#142).

2764.title: User Story (Requirements) candidate
2764.content: Captures a long list of features from an end-user’s perspective. It describes who the end-user is, with their feature wants or needs, and the reason for that want or need (see section 3.2.3). Also called: User Story, user story . PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 11). Internal and platform alternatives (smart-ra#133 S1): (1) PHC handbook §3.2.3 body (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-013-32-get-to-know-the-users.md, pp. 33-35): "User stories are the start of generating a long list of requirements, in non-technical terms, that will help the technical team to determine the more specific functional requirements of the system." and the template "“As a… [user persona], I want to… [do what I want to be able to do differently using an electronic system], so that… [reason for wanting that functionality].”" (2) Platform glossary `user-story` (folio-assistant-core/glossary/cat-harness.glossary.json), which binds the story to a Role rather than a user persona: "What a reader acting in a Role is trying to do, told as that role: as a <role>, I want <want>, so that <so that>." Also used as the functional requirements template ("As a … / I want … / So that ...") in SFP handbook §4.5 Table 12 (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-026-45-gather-requirements.md, page-043.md, p. 31).

2789.title: Health Management Information System (HMIS) candidate
2789.content: The Health Management Information System is a governed, shared application component responsible for the systematic collection, aggregation, analysis, and dissemination of population-level and facility-level health data to support health system planning, performance monitoring, resource allocation, and policy decision-making. Also called: HMIS . Lead sentence from Appendix C (Health Management Information System, 1 What It Is). Abbreviated HMIS throughout the RA draft and downstream Digital Transformation Handbooks. A candidate until the RA editors adopt it through the public review.

2794.title: Health Information System (HIS) candidate
2794.content: A system that integrates data collection, processing, reporting, and use of the information necessary for improving health service effectiveness and efficiency through better management at all levels of health services. Also called: HIS, health information system, Health Information System (HIS), Health Information Systems . DIIG Annex 1.1 Glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240010567-eng/sections/page-140.md, p. 128, citing WHO 2004 Developing health management information systems; also abbreviated in DIIG page-011.md and HRH handbook who-iris/library/9789240062627-eng/sections/page-006.md). The PHC handbook (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng) has no HIS abbreviation or definition; a wording earlier attributed to it here is not in its text and was removed (smart-ra#200). Referenced in SFP handbook glossary under SMART Guidelines (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-011.md, p. 11) and Ch. 4 (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-021-4-determine-the-requirements.md, page-035.md, p. 23). The definition is recorded as a candidate (smart-ra#133 S1, dth-sfp#1 P2).

2835.title: User Persona candidate
2835.content: A generic or archetypical profile of an end-user that is representative of a single type of end-user. Also called: Persona, persona, user persona . (2) SFP handbook glossary under 'Persona' (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-010.md, p. 10): "A generic aggregate description of a person involved in or benefiting from a health programme." All three are recorded as candidates; none is chosen.

2840.title: SNOMED GPS (SNOMED-GPS) candidate
2840.content: Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine – Global Patient Set is a list of basic clinical terms. It is an open and freely accessible subset of SNOMED CT terms that represents the breadth of concepts included in the SNOMED CT International Edition. Also called: SNOMED-GPS, Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine – Global Patient Set, Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine-Global Patient Set, GPS . The RA draft's own wording, verbatim. A candidate until the RA editors adopt it through the public review. Expanded in PHC handbook Abbreviations (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-001-abbreviations.md, pp. 7-8) as "SNOMED-GPS" = "Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine-Global Patient Set" and cited in SFP handbook §4.4 (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-025-44-outline-data-requirements.md, page-042.md, p. 30).

2860.title: Point-of-Service Applications (POS) candidate
2860.content: Point-of-service applications are end-user application components (IT systems or software tools) used by individuals directly engaged in healthcare—such as clinicians, community health workers, and patients—that enable interaction with the broader healthcare ecosystem. Also called: POS, Point-of-service applications, Point of Service Application, PoS . The RA draft's own wording, verbatim. A candidate until the RA editors adopt it through the public review. The draft marks this entry [Under review]. Also categorized in SFP handbook §3.2 Fig. 3 (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-020-32-link-to-the-enterprise-architecture.md, page-034.md, p. 22, citing DIIG) into reused POS applications and unique POS applications.

2875.title: Open Standards candidate
2875.content: Standards that are documented and made freely available to the public, which are developed, approved and maintained via a collaborative and consensus-driven process. Open standards facilitate interoperability and data exchange and are intended for widespread adoption (20). Also called: open standards, Open standards . PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 10), identical (with minor punctuation/citation differences) in PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-010.md, p. 10), and near-identical (two sentences) in SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "Standards that are documented and made freely available to the public. Open standards are developed, approved and maintained via a collaborative and consensus-driven process. Open standards facilitate interoperability and data exchange and are intended for widespread adoption (10)." Substantive/complementary alternative in RA §2.2.2 (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-022-222-the-enabling-conditions-for-reddhi.md, p. 35–39), citing Mehl et al. 2023 (library/mehl-2023-full-stac-oqad018/, linked via exactMatch to glossary/full-stac.glossary.json): "Open standards are validated and vetted specifications, repeatedly reusableacross contexts, that address common requirements, processes, and interactions and enable fidelity metrics." All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#142 item 3, smart-ra#143).

2987.title: Open Architectures candidate
2987.content: Documentation, using open standards, of reusable enterprise architecture patterns for health systems, describing the diverse digital interconnections of systems and capabilities (including trust networks, services, registries, access controls). Open architectures are designed to be instantiable via open technologies; provide a core infrastructure that fosters an ecosystem of digital health tools; are developed and maintained through collaborative, consensus-driven processes; and are freely available for use and adaptation without license restrictions. Transcribed from Figure 1 (p. 2). The figure's text is drawn as outlines, so the ingest could not extract it (vector-figures.json: vfig-p002 unrendered); the transcription was read off a 220 dpi render of the page on 2026-10-31 and needs a person to confirm it. Example given in the figure: the OpenHIE Architecture.

2997.content: Together, open Standards, open Technologies, open Architectures and open Content represent a next-generation ‘full-STAC’ remedy for digital health transformation. 3018.title: Open Standards candidate
3018.content: Semantic and syntactic models for data representation, exchange, and processing that ensure the precise meaning of exchanged information is unambiguously interpretable by any other system, service, or user. Open standards are developed and maintained through collaborative, consensus-driven processes, and are freely available for use and adaptation without license restrictions. Transcribed from Figure 1 (p. 2). The figure's text is drawn as outlines, so the ingest could not extract it (vector-figures.json: vfig-p002 unrendered); the transcription was read off a 220 dpi render of the page on 2026-10-31 and needs a person to confirm it. Example given in the figure: shared FHIR profiles with standard ontologies. The body text also says: 'OPEN STANDARDS refers to a common schema for health data, calculations and information exchange.' .

Actor (Conformance Model) candidate An Actor is an abstract, well-bounded role in the health information ecosystem that is defined entirely by the information-processing responsibilities it assumes and the interactions it participates in. An Actor is neither a software product nor an organisational unit. Defined in RA §3.7.2 (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-050-372-the-model.md, p. 111–116). Substantive distinction from the platform's `actor` concept in folio-assistant-core/glossary/cat-harness.glossary.json ("A concrete participant, human, agentic or mechanical, that persists across every process and takes on roles"): the RA's conformance-model Actor is an abstract information-processing role realised by concrete systems, closer to IHE's Actor or the platform's Role (smart-ra#133 S1). Adverse Events Following Immunization AEFI candidate Adverse effects following immunisation . Recorded per smart-ra#142 item 4: the PC handbook abbreviations list (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-006.md, p. 6) expands AEFI as "Adverse effects following immunisation", whereas standard WHO immunization terminology expands AEFI as "Adverse events following immunization" (an 'event' is any untoward medical occurrence following immunization and does not presuppose a causal 'effect'). Both expansions are recorded as candidates; neither is silently altered. Enabling Environment candidate Attitudes, actions, policies and practices that stimulate and support effective and efficient functioning of organizations, individuals and programmes. The enabling environment includes legal, regulatory and policy frameworks and political, sociocultural, institutional and economic factors (3). SFP handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-009.md, p. 9, citing DIIG), matching DIIG Annex 1.1 Glossary (who-iris/library/9789240010567-eng/sections/page-139.md, p. 127). End-User candidate People who will be using the digital system(s). Identical wording in PHC handbook glossary ('End-user', who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 8), PC handbook glossary ('End user', who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8), and SFP handbook glossary ('End user', who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9). Enterprise Architecture EA candidate The organising logic for business processes and IT infrastructure reflecting the integration and standardisation requirements of the organisation's operating model. The RA draft's own glossary wording, verbatim (folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md); the draft marks this entry [Under review]. (2) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8, citing DIIG): "A blueprint of business processes, data, systems and technologies that helps planners, software developers and managers design increasingly complex systems to support the workflow and roles of people in a large enterprise such as a health system (1)." (3) SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9, citing DIIG): "A blueprint of business processes, data, systems and technologies used to help implementers design increasingly complex systems to support the workflow and roles of people in a large enterprise, such as a health system (3)." Evaluation candidate The systematic and objective assessment of an ongoing or completed intervention with the aim of determining the fulfilment of objectives, efficiency, effectiveness, impact and sustainability (8). SFP handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-009.md, p. 9, citing Monitoring and evaluating digital health interventions, WHO 2016). 3029.content: Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources FHIR candidate FHIR is a standard for healthcare data exchange, published by HL7® . The RA draft's own wording, verbatim. A candidate until the RA editors adopt it through the public review. Term page · Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H · https://litlfred.github.io/smart-ra/v0/ns/glossary/dpi-h-ra/fast-healthcare-interoperability-resources · source folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md . Features candidate The characteristics of a system that include look and feel as well as what the system can do (e.g. “reporting” can be a feature of a PCPOSS). PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 9). Wording alternatives across the DTH corpus, differing only in domain example and 'a system' vs 'your system' (smart-ra#133 S1): (1) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "The characteristics of a system that include look and feel as well as what the system can do (e.g., “order processing” can be a feature of an order management solution)." (2) PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "The characteristics of your system that include look and feel as well as what the system can do (e.g., “approval workflow” can be a feature of a product master data management solution)." All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen. Candidate definitions (2) . | Functions (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Functions in a system are how features are implemented (e.g. “calculating aggregate data” and “displaying feedback in the form of diagrams” are functions of the “reporting” feature of a PCPOSS). PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 9). Substantive alternative in SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "Business processes within a system that help the system perform (e.g., “receiving inventory” and “picking inventory” are functions of the “warehousing” feature of a warehouse management system)." (PHC defines functions as "how features are implemented"; SC defines them as "Business processes within a system that help the system perform".) Both are recorded as candidates; neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1). | Functional Requirements (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Description of what the digital system needs to do to support the tasks that make up the health system process and address the identified health system challenges (e.g. a PCPOSS must be able to remind health workers which health service users to follow-up with). PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 9). Wording and substantive alternatives across the DTH corpus (smart-ra#133 S1): (1) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "A description of what the digital system needs to do to support the tasks that make up the business process and address the identified challenges." (2) PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8): "Description of what the digital system needs to do to support the tasks that make up the health system process and address the identified challenges (e.g., a product master data management solution must be able to define categories and attributes to organize product information)." (3) SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "Capabilities the system must have to meet the end users’ needs and achieve tasks within the business process." All four are recorded as candidates; none is chosen. | . Foundational Digital Public Infrastructure DPI-F candidate Foundational Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI-F) is the digital public infrastructure, such as identity, payments and data exchange, upon which the health sector can build. DPI-H is distinct from DPI-F and builds on it. Added to the RA glossary table in CS-001 (smart-ra#185, public comments No. 136 and No. 327), per committee feedback (CL). A candidate until the RA editors adopt it through the public review. Named in the RA draft's Acronyms table, which gives the expansion used as prefLabel, and in Section 1.2.3 on cross-sectoral foundational DPI (digital identity, payments, data exchange). Full-STAC candidate An ecosystem specifying open standards, open technologies, open architectures, and open content (full-STAC). Cites Mehl et al. 2023 (library/mehl-2023-full-stac-oqad018/, glossary/full-stac.glossary.json) in RA §2.2.2 (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-022-222-the-enabling-conditions-for-reddhi.md). Linked via exactMatch to the full-STAC scheme (smart-ra#143). Candidate definitions (4) . | Open Standards (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Standards that are documented and made freely available to the public, which are developed, approved and maintained via a collaborative and consensus-driven process. Open standards facilitate interoperability and data exchange and are intended for widespread adoption (20). PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 10), identical (with minor punctuation/citation differences) in PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-010.md, p. 10), and near-identical (two sentences) in SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "Standards that are documented and made freely available to the public. Open standards are developed, approved and maintained via a collaborative and consensus-driven process. Open standards facilitate interoperability and data exchange and are intended for widespread adoption (10)." Substantive/complementary alternative in RA §2.2.2 (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-022-222-the-enabling-conditions-for-reddhi.md, p. 35–39), citing Mehl et al. 2023 (library/mehl-2023-full-stac-oqad018/, linked via exactMatch to glossary/full-stac.glossary.json): "Open standards are validated and vetted specifications, repeatedly reusableacross contexts, that address common requirements, processes, and interactions and enable fidelity metrics." All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#142 item 3, smart-ra#143). | Open Technologies (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Open technologies denote components of configurable and extensible source code — often curated as digital public goods — that perform distinct functions while adhering to open standards. RA §2.2.2 body wording, verbatim (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-022-222-the-enabling-conditions-for-reddhi.md, p. 35–39), citing Mehl et al. 2023 (library/mehl-2023-full-stac-oqad018/, glossary/full-stac.glossary.json: "Components of configurable and extensible source code, often curated as 'global goods' or 'digital public goods', that perform a distinct function while adhering to open standards."). Linked via exactMatch to the full-STAC scheme (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#143). | Open Architectures (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Open architectures refer to high-level specifications of technical designs that provide blueprints for creating open ecosystems structured into reusable and shareable components. RA §2.2.2 body wording, verbatim (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-022-222-the-enabling-conditions-for-reddhi.md, p. 35–39), citing Mehl et al. 2023 (library/mehl-2023-full-stac-oqad018/, glossary/full-stac.glossary.json: "High-level specifications of technical designs that provide blueprints for creating open ecosystems structured into reusable and shareable components, such as within a health information exchange."). Linked via exactMatch to the full-STAC scheme (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#143). | Open Content (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Open content refers to domain ideas and synthesized knowledge clearly documented without restrictions inhibiting readability or usage. RA §2.2.2 body wording, verbatim (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-022-222-the-enabling-conditions-for-reddhi.md, p. 35–39), citing Mehl et al. 2023 (library/mehl-2023-full-stac-oqad018/, glossary/full-stac.glossary.json: "Domain ideas and synthesized knowledge clearly documented without restrictions inhibiting readability or usage, such as health guidelines, workflows, core data elements, terminology mappings, and test cases aligned to standards."). Linked via exactMatch to the full-STAC scheme (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#143). | . Quoted from the abstract. The paper calls it both an approach and a remedy, and names the four as 'four factors'. The DPI-H RA draft (sec-022, footnote 14) cites this paper and presents the four as 'the enabling conditions for REDDHI'. 3030.content: Generic Product candidate In this handbook, the terms ‘generic product,’ ‘product,’ or ‘product information’ pertain to the general identifying details of a health product, excluding any manufacturer-specific information. PC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8), identical in SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-010.md, p. 10). Internal wording alternative in PC handbook Ch. 2 body (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-028.md, p. 28): "Generic products can be described as generic items that conceal the brand or manufacturer information." Distinct from the RA's architectural `product` concept; both wordings are recorded as candidates and neither is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#142). Candidate definitions (2) . | Trade Item (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Trade items are manufacturer-specific branded health products that are identifiable and unique to a particular brand or manufacturer. Owner decision 2026-10-31 (smart-ra#142 item 1, smart-ra#139): Trade Item is the shared WHO concept with this narrow definition from the Product Catalogue handbook Ch. 2 body (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-028.md, p. 28). The GS1 trade item is a separate external concept and the WHO term's broadMatch (every WHO Trade Item is a GS1 trade item, not the reverse: GS1's also covers services). The PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-011.md, p. 11) print the GS1 wording — "Products or services that are priced, ordered or invoiced at any point in the supply chain" — citing GS1 (PC ref. 13, SFP ref. 19); that sentence is recorded here as a note citing GS1, not as the WHO concept's definition. | Product Master Data (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Product master data consists of standardized information that accurately describes a health product’s characteristics. This data remains consistent across all instances of a product. PC handbook Introduction wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-010.md, p. 10). Shared concept across PC (9789240116191-eng), SC (9789240101197-eng), and SFP (9789240120747-eng). Per owner decision 2026-10-31 (smart-ra#141, smart-ra#142): one concept, with no homonym split needed against the RA's architectural `product` concept. | . 3036.content: Open Architectures candidate Open architectures refer to high-level specifications of technical designs that provide blueprints for creating open ecosystems structured into reusable and shareable components. Candidate definitions (4) . | Full-STAC (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)An ecosystem specifying open standards, open technologies, open architectures, and open content (full-STAC). Cites Mehl et al. 2023 (library/mehl-2023-full-stac-oqad018/, glossary/full-stac.glossary.json) in RA §2.2.2 (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-022-222-the-enabling-conditions-for-reddhi.md). Linked via exactMatch to the full-STAC scheme (smart-ra#143). | Open Standards (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Standards that are documented and made freely available to the public, which are developed, approved and maintained via a collaborative and consensus-driven process. Open standards facilitate interoperability and data exchange and are intended for widespread adoption (20). PHC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 10), identical (with minor punctuation/citation differences) in PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-010.md, p. 10), and near-identical (two sentences) in SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "Standards that are documented and made freely available to the public. Open standards are developed, approved and maintained via a collaborative and consensus-driven process. Open standards facilitate interoperability and data exchange and are intended for widespread adoption (10)." Substantive/complementary alternative in RA §2.2.2 (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-022-222-the-enabling-conditions-for-reddhi.md, p. 35–39), citing Mehl et al. 2023 (library/mehl-2023-full-stac-oqad018/, linked via exactMatch to glossary/full-stac.glossary.json): "Open standards are validated and vetted specifications, repeatedly reusableacross contexts, that address common requirements, processes, and interactions and enable fidelity metrics." All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#142 item 3, smart-ra#143). | Open Technologies (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Open technologies denote components of configurable and extensible source code — often curated as digital public goods — that perform distinct functions while adhering to open standards. RA §2.2.2 body wording, verbatim (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-022-222-the-enabling-conditions-for-reddhi.md, p. 35–39), citing Mehl et al. 2023 (library/mehl-2023-full-stac-oqad018/, glossary/full-stac.glossary.json: "Components of configurable and extensible source code, often curated as 'global goods' or 'digital public goods', that perform a distinct function while adhering to open standards."). Linked via exactMatch to the full-STAC scheme (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#143). | Open Content (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)Open content refers to domain ideas and synthesized knowledge clearly documented without restrictions inhibiting readability or usage. RA §2.2.2 body wording, verbatim (library/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/sections/sec-022-222-the-enabling-conditions-for-reddhi.md, p. 35–39), citing Mehl et al. 2023 (library/mehl-2023-full-stac-oqad018/, glossary/full-stac.glossary.json: "Domain ideas and synthesized knowledge clearly documented without restrictions inhibiting readability or usage, such as health guidelines, workflows, core data elements, terminology mappings, and test cases aligned to standards."). Linked via exactMatch to the full-STAC scheme (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#143). | . Open Architectures candidate Documentation, using open standards, of reusable enterprise architecture patterns for health systems, describing the diverse digital interconnections of systems and capabilities (including trust networks, services, registries, access controls). Open architectures are designed to be instantiable via open technologies; provide a core infrastructure that fosters an ecosystem of digital health tools; are developed and maintained through collaborative, consensus-driven processes; and are freely available for use and adaptation without license restrictions. Transcribed from Figure 1 (p. 2). Candidate definitions (2) . | Generic Product (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)In this handbook, the terms ‘generic product,’ ‘product,’ or ‘product information’ pertain to the general identifying details of a health product, excluding any manufacturer-specific information. PC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8), identical in SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-010.md, p. 10). SMART Guidelines SMART candidate Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based, Testable Guidelines are a comprehensive set of reusable digital health components (e.g., interoperability standards, code libraries, algorithms, technical and operational specifications) that transform the guideline adaptation and implementation process to preserve fidelity and accelerate uptake. SMART Guidelines provide a five-step pathway to advance the adoption of best clinical and data practices, even if a country is not yet fully digital. The RA draft's own glossary wording, verbatim (folio/dpi-h-ra/glossary/t-glossary-lead-a31853.md). Substantive and wording alternatives across the DTH corpus (smart-ra#133 S1, smart-ra#139, smart-ra#140, smart-ra#142): (1) PHC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, p. 11) and SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/page-011.md, p. 11): "Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based, and Testable Guidelines are recommended digital capabilities, health and data content aligned with normative recommendations. They represent packages of comprehensive documentation and reusable digital health components (e.g. health content, interoperability standards, code libraries, algorithms, technical and operational specifications) that facilitate country adaptation and adoption of clinical and public health protocols, health systems strengthening recommendations, and data and interoperability standards into digital health information systems with fidelity. SMART Guidelines serve as a starting point and as foundational specifications to advance the development of robust person-centred digital systems. These specifications are software-agnostic, context-agnostic, and are applicable to all levels of digital maturity (10,23)." (2) SC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240101197-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "The WHO guidelines for developing Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based and Testable components for implementing digital health capabilities. The components include interoperability standards, code libraries, algorithms, and technical and operational specifications. The SMART Guidelines provide a five-step pathway to advance the adoption of best clinical and data practices, even if a country is not yet fully digital (12, 13)." (3) PC handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-009.md, p. 9): "WHO standards-based, machine-readable, adaptive, requirements-based, and testable Guidelines are recommended digital capabilities, health and data content. They represent a comprehensive set of reusable digital health components (e.g., interoperability standards, code libraries, algorithms, technical and operational specifications) that transform the guideline adaptation and implementation process to preserve fidelity and accelerate uptake. SMART Guidelines provide a five-step pathway to advance the adoption of best clinical and data practices, even if a country is not yet fully digital.11, 12" All are recorded as candidates; none is chosen. Owner decision 2026-10-31 (smart-ra#142 item 1, smart-ra#139): Trade Item is the shared WHO concept with this narrow definition from the Product Catalogue handbook Ch. 2 body (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-028.md, p. 28). The GS1 trade item is a separate external concept and the WHO term's broadMatch (every WHO Trade Item is a GS1 trade item, not the reverse: GS1's also covers services). Candidate definitions (2) . | Generic Product (Glossary of the Reference Architecture and Guidance for DPI-H)In this handbook, the terms ‘generic product,’ ‘product,’ or ‘product information’ pertain to the general identifying details of a health product, excluding any manufacturer-specific information. PC handbook glossary wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-008.md, p. 8), identical in SFP handbook glossary (who-iris/library/9789240120747-eng/sections/sec-002-glossary.md, page-010.md, p. 10). Internal wording alternative in PC handbook Ch. 2 body (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-028.md, p. 28): "Generic products can be described as generic items that conceal the brand or manufacturer information." This data remains consistent across all instances of a product. PC handbook Introduction wording, verbatim (who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng/sections/page-010.md, p. 10). Shared concept across PC (9789240116191-eng), SC (9789240101197-eng), and SFP (9789240120747-eng). Per owner decision 2026-10-31 (smart-ra#141, smart-ra#142): one concept, with no homonym split needed against the RA's architectural `product` concept. | . 3106.title: translations — review
3106.content: Every catalogue in every locale, and whether a person has reviewed it. Tick the machine translations you find acceptable, or open mistranslation… on a cell to suggest better text for its strings, then press Submit. That opens a GitHub issue prefilled with your review. Filing it makes you, by your GitHub login, the reviewer, and a workflow turns it into a pull request recording your verdict. Owners, members and collaborators of a layer's repository can adjudicate it. Submitting needs JavaScript; the table reads without it. A suggestion is applied as a #, fuzzy string and flags the catalogue for review: nobody else has reviewed your text yet. Accepting sets the catalogue reviewed, pinned to the version you saw, and it shows as stale once that catalogue changes. Coverage numbers are on the status page.
